**Flow** is how a rapper fits words to the beat. Kyle Adams, a music theorist, defines it as "all of the ways
in which a rapper uses rhythm and articulation in his/her lyrical delivery" (Adams [1]). This lesson covers the
rhythm side: where the syllables, accents and rhymes land in the bar. It also covers what researchers have found
about how flow changed between the late 1970s and today.

The reading list for this lesson, with notes on what each source covers and how much of it was read for this
page, is [Rap Flow 2: Reading list](rap-flow-reading.qmd).

::: {.rf-note}
**About the examples.** Every pattern on this page was made up for this page to show a technique that a source
describes. None of them is a transcription of a record, and the made-up lines are not quotations. Each pattern
says which source it follows. The sound is a click for each syllable (higher for rhymes, louder for accents)
over a simple drum loop.
:::

## What you'll do

- Read a **flow grid**, the 16-box chart that rappers and researchers both use.
- Hear the steady, on-the-beat style of early rap, then the busier styles that followed.
- Hear rhymes that make a cross-rhythm against the beat, and sentences that run across the bar line.
- Hear **triplet flow**, and the difference between rapping on the grid and off it.
- Weigh what the research says about whether rap got "more complex".
- Build a flow of your own.

## The grid: 16 boxes to a bar

Most rap is in 4/4. Each beat splits into four sixteenths, so a bar has sixteen places a syllable can land.
Counted aloud that's *1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a*. Adams draws his charts this way: one row per bar, one
box per sixteenth, the syllables written in their boxes (Adams, note 2). Mitchell Ohriner points out that rap
teachers and rappers use the same picture. Rakim describes drawing sixteen dots per bar, and Paul Edwards's
*How to Rap* says a stressed syllable should fall on each of the four beats (Ohriner [1.3]–[1.4]).

How to read the grids below:

- A box with **•** has a syllable. A bold **●** is an accented one.
- **Coloured** boxes rhyme. The same colour means the same rhyme sound.
- The staff under the grid shows the same rhythm on one line, as a drum part would be written. Rhymes are
  lettered above the notes and accents are marked >.

## Early rap: square and on the beat

Adams contrasts Kurtis Blow's "Basketball" (1984) with a 1995 verse by RZA. In "Basketball" the rhythm is
"square, regular", the beat is never split finer than a sixteenth, and the rhymes come in couplets in
predictable places (Adams [3]). A rhymed couplet on the **fourth beat** was a trademark of early-1980s rappers
(Adams [4]). Sentences also tend to match the bars: one sentence per bar, or a 1 + 1 + 2 pattern over four bars
(Adams [24]).

<div class="rf" data-title="Square flow, rhyme on beat 4 (after Adams [3]–[4]; made-up words)" data-bpm="96"
  data-bars="X.x.X.x.XxxxA... | X.x.X.x.XxxxA..."
  data-words="I step to the mic and rock the place the crowd jumps up all o ver the space"></div>

Every beat has a stressed syllable, the rhyme lands on beat 4, and each line fills exactly one bar.

Adams warns against using this as a ranking. Early rappers were often improvising, and they needed "rhythmic
formulae into which they could plug their syllables" (Adams [33]). He calls flow complexity a matter of style,
not a "yardstick" for judging rappers (Adams [35]).

### The beat-4 rhyme never went away

Nathaniel Condit-Schultz's MCFlow corpus transcribes 124 Billboard rap tracks from 1980 to 2015. As Robert
Komaniecki reports its results, the typical pace is about 4.5 syllables per second, about a quarter of stressed
syllables rhyme, and rhymed syllables land on **beat 4** more often than anywhere else (Komaniecki [1.2]).

At 90 BPM a beat lasts two-thirds of a second, so 4.5 syllables per second works out to about three syllables
per beat. (That arithmetic is this page's. The MCFlow paper itself was not read for this page.)

## Getting busier: rhymes against the beat

Adams's 2002 example, Blackalicious's "Blazing Arrow", has almost no empty boxes. In twelve bars of steady
sixteenths, "only five sixteenth-note beats do not have attacks" (Adams [11]). The interest comes from the
rhymes. They come in **three-sixteenth units**, three to a line, and the first and last syllable of each unit
rhyme (Adams [13]). Groups of three sixteenths don't line up with beats of four, so the rhymes make a
cross-rhythm against the beat. In later bars the units move to start at other points in the bar (Adams [15]).

<div class="rf" data-title="Steady sixteenths, rhymes in 3-sixteenth units (after Adams [11]–[15]; not his transcription)" data-bpm="88"
  data-bars="AxaAxaAxaxxxxxxx | AxaAxaAxaxxxxxxx | xxAxaAxaAxaxxxxx | xxAxaAxaAxaxxxxx"></div>

Count along. In bars 1–2 the rhyme groups start on the beat. In bars 3–4 they start an eighth note later, so the
same rhythm feels different against the drums.

## Accents against the beat: 4 against 3

In Dr. Dre's verse on N.W.A.'s "100 Miles and Runnin'" (1990), Adams finds most accents on the beat or halfway
between beats. One bar is the exception: it puts four accents across the last three beats, a 4-against-3
pattern (Adams [30]–[31]). Four evenly spaced accents across three beats come out one every three sixteenths.

<div class="rf" data-title="Four accents over three beats, then back on the beat (after Adams [30]–[31])" data-bpm="92"
  data-bars="X.x.X.x.X.x.A... | x.x.XxxXxxXxxXx. | X.x.X.x.X.x.A... | x.x.XxxXxxXxxA.."></div>

## Sentences across the bar line

The third technique on Adams's list is how well a rapper's sentences line up with the bars (Adams [8]). When a
sentence runs on past a bar line, that's **enjambment**, which Adams defines as "a syntactic connection that
overrides a metrical boundary" (Adams [4]). In MF DOOM's "All Caps" (2004), only 11 of 20 bars end with the end
of a sentence, and only five lines are exactly one bar long (Adams [24]). Most end-rhymes still land around beat
4, but the internal rhymes move around unpredictably (Adams [22]). Adams says the drums mark the meter clearly
enough that the voice doesn't have to (Adams [25]).

<div class="rf" data-title="Phrases that start and stop mid-bar, rhymes off the beat (after Adams [22]–[25])" data-bpm="90"
  data-bars="..xxxxAx.xxxxxbx | xxx.xaxx..xxBxxx | x..xxxxAxxx.xxxx | xbxx.xx.xaxx...."></div>

Compare this with the first example. There, every line started on beat 1 and ended on beat 4. Here, the gaps
between phrases fall in the middle of bars, and the rhymes land on the off-beats.

## Triplet flow

Triplet flow splits each beat into **three** instead of four. Ben Duinker calls it "one of the most aurally
salient features of contemporary hip hop" and links it to Atlanta trap music, with its "sparse, slow beats". He
names Cardi B, Kendrick Lamar, Drake, Big Sean and Young Thug as rappers who use it (Duinker, abstract). He
argues that rappers of the late 1980s and early 1990s provided the "stylistic blueprint" for its later spread.
His reference list includes Bone Thugs-n-Harmony and Three 6 Mafia from the mid-1990s, and Migos's "Versace"
(2013). He defines three kinds of triplet flow: mixed, phrasal and total. (Only the abstract and reference list
were read here, so the details of those three kinds aren't given.) Ohriner also notes triplet flow as the
recognised exception to the 16-box grid, "now commonly associated" with Atlanta (Ohriner [1.5]).

<div class="rf" data-title="Triplet flow: 12 boxes to a bar, over a half-time trap beat (made up for this page)" data-bpm="72" data-beat="trap"
  data-bars="t:xxaxxaxxaxx. | t:xxaxxaxxa... | t:xxbxxbxxbxx. | t:xxbxxbxxb..."></div>

Switch the beat to boom-bap and back. The same triplets feel different over the two drum patterns.

## On the grid, or off it

The grids assume every syllable lands exactly in a box. Ohriner measured real recordings and found that this
isn't always true. He separates two kinds of delivery (Ohriner [1.5], [2.1]–[2.5]):

- **Music-rhythmic** delivery has syllables close to the sixteenth-note grid, with lengths near a quarter of a
  beat.
- **Speech-rhythmic** delivery has lengths that vary like speech, often slowing down across a phrase.

He measures how far a rapper sits from the grid. In one line of Kendrick Lamar's "Momma" the delivery is
music-rhythmic but about a sixteenth **behind the beat**. Another line is speech-rhythmic and speeds up, then
slows down (Ohriner [3.3]–[3.6]).

<div class="rf" data-title="The same phrase on the grid, then pulled off it (the slider is a sketch of Ohriner's description, not his measurements)" data-bpm="90" data-drift="0"
  data-bars="..xxxxxxxxxxxxxx | xxxxxxa......... | ..xxxxxxxxxxxxxx | xxxxxxa........."></div>

Play it with the slider at 0, then at about 0.5. The syllables are the same, but they start late and slow down
through each phrase, more like talking than drumming.

## Did rap get more complex?

Many writers have claimed that rap flow became steadily more complex. Adam Krims described a move from
"old-school" flow in the early to mid-1980s to "new-school" flow from the mid-1990s. The new style had more
internal and off-beat rhymes, more syncopation, and "violations of meter" (Krims, as Adams [6] quotes him). Krims
also named three styles: *sung*, *percussion-effusive* and *speech-effusive* (Adams [6]).

Adam Waller tested this claim. He transcribed 45 verses from 1979 to 2009, one per artist, from Grandmaster
Flash and Sugarhill Gang to Young Jeezy and Cam'ron (Waller, Fig. 4.1, p. 110). He scored each verse with models
of syncopation and rhythmic repetition that he had checked against listeners' ratings of complexity. His
findings:

- In every model, complexity rose from the mid-1980s (at the latest) through the 1990s, and the verses from that
  period agreed closely with each other (Waller, p. 127).
- At or within a couple of years of **2000**, the rise stopped and turned toward *less* complexity
  (Waller, p. 128).
- After 2000, the verses spread much more widely. Some of the most complex verses in his set come from that
  period, such as Aesop Rock and DOOM. He concludes that recent rap is best understood as "fragmentation of the
  genre into a wider variety of styles" (Waller, pp. 128–129).
- So the idea of a steady rise in complexity "is unsustainable" (Waller, p. 128). The commonly cited increase
  "has some validity, but is more complicated than is often suggested" (Waller, p. 130).

Komaniecki tracks a different change: who raps together. In the 1980s and early 1990s, groups like Run-D.M.C.,
the Beastie Boys and A Tribe Called Quest dominated, and group members often shared one unified flow. Later, the
usual set-up became a solo artist with guest rappers (Komaniecki [0.4], section 2).

Pitch has changed too. Komaniecki describes a range from "the imprecise and exaggerated declamatory features of
speech" in early rap to "carefully-pitched singing" in modern flows (Komaniecki, "Vocal Pitch", abstract).

### A rough timeline

The dates come from the sources above. Where a source gives a range, the range is shown. This is a summary of
those sources, not a full history.

| When | What changes in the flow | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Late 1970s – mid-1980s | Square rhythms, couplet rhymes on beat 4, one sentence per bar ("old school") | Adams [3]–[4], [24]; Krims in Adams [6] |
| 1980s – early 1990s | Groups with unified flows (Run-D.M.C., De La Soul) | Komaniecki section 2 |
| Mid-1980s – 1990s | Complexity rises: off-beat and internal rhymes, syncopation, enjambment ("new school", speech-effusive) | Waller p. 127; Krims in Adams [6] |
| Late 1980s – mid-1990s | Triplet rhythms in some rappers' flows, the "blueprint" for triplet flow | Duinker, abstract |
| Around 2000 | The rise in complexity stops; styles spread out | Waller pp. 128–129 |
| 2010s | Triplet flow everywhere, tied to trap's slow, sparse beats | Duinker, abstract |
| 2010s | Solo rappers with features rather than groups | Komaniecki [0.4] |

## Build a flow

Click a box to cycle it through: empty → syllable → accent → rhyme *a* → rhyme *b* → empty. Then press Play.

<div class="rf" data-edit data-title="Your flow" data-bpm="90"
  data-bars="................ | ................ | ................ | ................"></div>

Things to try:

1. Write a square, old-school couplet: a stressed syllable on every beat and the rhyme on beat 4.
2. Keep the same rhymes, but start each line on the *a* of beat 4 in the bar before.
3. Fill a bar with sixteenths and add rhymes every three boxes. Where do they land in the next bar?
4. Write a line of your own over the grid. Clap the beat and say it until the syllables sit in their boxes.

## Check yourself

1. What are the three *metrical* techniques of flow on Adams's list that this page shows?
2. Why do rhymes in groups of three sixteenths feel like they are pulling against the beat?
3. What is enjambment, and what does Adams say lets rappers get away with it?
4. What is the difference between Ohriner's music-rhythmic and speech-rhythmic delivery?
5. Waller found the rise in complexity stopped around 2000. What happened to the verses after that?
6. Why does Adams refuse to use flow as a "yardstick" for rappers?

<details><summary>Answers</summary>

1. Where the rhymes go, where the accents go, and how well sentences line up with bars. The fourth on his list
   is the number of syllables per beat (Adams [8]).
2. Three doesn't divide four. The groups start in a different place in each beat, so the rhyme pattern lines
   up with the beat only every three beats.
3. A sentence running on past a bar line. The drum beat marks the meter clearly enough that the voice doesn't
   have to (Adams [25]).
4. Music-rhythmic delivery sits close to the sixteenth grid with even lengths. Speech-rhythmic delivery has
   uneven, speech-like lengths, often slowing down across a phrase.
5. On average they moved toward less complexity, but they spread out much more: some very complex verses and
   some simple ones.
6. Early rappers were often improvising and may not have aimed for complex flow. A simple flow can be a style,
   not a failing (Adams [33]–[35]).

</details>
